title: Session 3: Correlative Conjunctions
summary: The most common correlative conjunctions — both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, whether … or, not … but, rather … than — with the balance rule, verb agreement and punctuation. Plus a review of FANBOYS and subordinating conjunctions.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you can …
items: Use the common correlative pairs with the right meaning
Keep the same kind of word after each half of the pair
Choose the right verb after either … or / neither … nor / both … and
Review: choose correctly between FANBOYS and subordinating conjunctions

blocks.title: Sessions 1 and 2 in four lines
items: **IC, FANBOYS IC** — The shop was closed, so we went home.
**DC, IC** — Because the shop was closed, we went home.
**IC DC** — We went home because the shop was closed.
One link = one joining word: ✗ although … but ✗ because … so.

blocks.text: Correlative conjunctions are **pairs** of joining words. The two parts work together: one part comes before the first idea and the other part comes before the second idea.

rows: You can **either** call me **or** send a message.
not the first and not the second
**Neither** the teacher **nor** the students knew the answer.
addition with emphasis (the second idea is even more impressive)
She is **not only** a good student **but also** a talented artist.
it does not matter which; or a question of two choices
I'll finish the essay **whether** it rains **or** not.
correcting: the second idea is the true one
The problem is **not** the cost **but** the time.
I **would rather** walk **than** take the bus.

blocks.title: Rule 1 — Balance: the same kind of word after each half
items: Look at what comes **directly after** each part of the pair. It should be the same kind of word (noun + noun, verb + verb, adjective + adjective).
✗ She is **not only** clever **but also** works hard. (adjective / verb)
✓ She is **not only** clever **but also** hard-working. (adjective / adjective)
✓ She **not only** studies hard **but also** helps her classmates. (verb / verb)

blocks.title: Rule 2 — Verb agreement
items: **both … and** → the subject is plural: Both my brother and my sister **are** doctors.
**either … or / neither … nor** → the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: Neither the teacher nor **the students were** ready. · Either the students or **the teacher has** the key.

blocks.title: Rule 3 — Neither … nor is already negative
items: ✗ I **don't** like **neither** tea **nor** coffee.
✓ I like **neither** tea **nor** coffee. = ✓ I don't like **either** tea **or** coffee.

blocks.title: Rule 4 — Not only at the start of a sentence
items: When Not only starts the sentence and joins two clauses, the word order changes (like a question): **Not only + auxiliary + subject**.
She won the race. She broke the record. → **Not only did she** win the race, **but she also** broke the record.
This is a strong structure for academic writing, but use it once, not in every paragraph.

blocks.title: Rule 5 — Punctuation
items: When the pair joins **words or phrases**, use **no comma**: You can either email or phone me.
When the pair joins **two full clauses**, put a comma before the second part: Either you apologise, or I will tell the teacher. · Not only did the plan fail, but it also cost a lot of money.

rows: both … and · not only … but also
although, though, even though, whereas, while

items.q: Complete: ___ Cairo and Alexandria are on the Nile Delta.
Complete: You can ___ stay here or come with us.
Complete: ___ the manager nor his assistant answered the phone.
Complete: The film was not only long ___ boring.
Choose the verb: Neither the players nor the coach (was / were) happy.
Choose the verb: Both the house and the garden (needs / need) repairs.
Correct: He doesn't eat neither meat nor fish.
items.a: He eats neither meat nor fish. / He doesn't eat either meat or fish.

items.q: Correct: She is not only smart but also she is kind.
items.a: She is not only smart but also kind. (balance)

items.q: Rewrite with **Not only**: The storm damaged houses. It also destroyed the bridge.
items.a: Not only did the storm damage houses, but it also destroyed the bridge.

items.q: Join with a **subordinating** conjunction: It was late. We kept working.
items.a: Although it was late, we kept working.

items.q: Join with **FANBOYS**: He didn't call. He didn't write.
items.a: He didn't call, nor did he write.

questions.q: Neither the students nor the teacher ___ the answer.
questions.e: The verb agrees with the nearer subject (the teacher).

questions.e: Two full clauses → comma before or.

questions.q: Which joining word could replace but in It was cold, but we swam?
c: Because it was cold, we swam.
Although it was cold, we swam.
So it was cold, we swam.
Either it was cold or we swam.
